extracted.intended_audience: NPR readers and the general public interested in technology and public policy
extracted.subtask_short: report on FCC net neutrality comments
extracted.subtask_description: A news article reporting that John Oliver's television segment prompted a large volume of public comments to the FCC about net neutrality, describing the submission channels, scale, timeline, and the policy issue at stake.

rubrics_metrics.name: Submission channels for public comment
rubrics_metrics.description: The FCC accepts comments through an official electronic commenting system and, separately, via a special inbox the agency set up for public emails.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article notes the distinction and volumes: the official electronic commenting system received more than 45,000 comments since May 15, while a separate special inbox received 300,000 emails. It also reports that the official system experienced "technical difficulties" due to heavy traffic, indicating that choice of channel and system capacity can affect delivery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timeliness — observe the commenting period deadline
rubrics_metrics.description: Comments must be filed during the open commenting period; the article states the current commenting period runs through June 27.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The piece gives timeline context (open commenting period opened May 15 and runs through June 27), implying that submissions after the deadline will not be part of the record for that rulemaking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand the policy issue being commented on (net neutrality and 'fast lanes')
rubrics_metrics.description: Net neutrality is defined as the principle that data on the Internet should be served on a level playing field without prejudice for companies that can pay to get content delivered faster.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article explains what's 'on the table': a proposal that could allow ISPs to charge for 'fast lanes,' potentially disadvantaging startups and altering the competitive landscape; it notes that major tech companies and activists have spoken out against the proposal. Understanding these specifics helps inform the substance of a comment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scale and public mobilization matter
rubrics_metrics.description: Large volumes of public comments can draw attention and overwhelm agency systems; a celebrity-driven call to action can massively increase comment counts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For context the article contrasts the >45,000 formal comments and 300,000 emails with the next-highest number of formal comments on an FCC measure (just under 2,000). It also recounts that the influx caused the FCC to tweet about technical difficulties, illustrating how scale can affect the process and visibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Messaging and call-to-action effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Public figures can influence turnout and the tone of submissions; Oliver's plea moved viewers to act and framed the action as focusing 'indiscriminate rage in a useful direction.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While not prescriptive about comment content, the article highlights that framing from media/celebrity can convert viewers into commenters and shape public participation patterns.
